channel.title: Signal Brief · The Signal
channel.description: Signal Brief: the day in technology, in The Signal's own words. Every item is written from linked official sources and fact checked before publication.

item.title: Perplexity launches always on work agents called Teammates
item.description: Perplexity has launched Teammates, always on AI agents built for work that can take on different roles in a workspace at the same time. Each Teammate works from its own thread in the Perplexity app and can draw on existing projects, skills and memory, and users can talk to them in Slack. Access is limited to the $200 a month Max plan, and chief executive Aravind Srinivas said on X that he sees organisations eventually having hundreds of Teammates working for each person. Why it matters for tech: Work agents are moving from single chatbots to teams of agents with their own roles, and Perplexity is charging a premium for the shift.

item.title: Meta Muse can now build custom spaces from a description
item.description: Meta has added spaces to its Muse assistant, letting users describe an app such as a shopping hub, a school dashboard or a trivia game and have Muse build it. Connected apps such as Gmail, Google Calendar, OpenTable and Notion let Muse keep the details in a space current in the background, and users can tick items off, add notes and place spaces in the sidebar or on a schedule. Meta also said Active Memory and Active Focus, capabilities from its Muse Wonder model, are coming to the Muse app and the Meta AI chatbot. Why it matters for tech: Assistants are turning into personalised workspaces that stay current on their own, which raises the bar for what a chatbot is expected to do.

item.title: Cognition ships a cheaper coding model but keeps its weights private
item.description: Cognition has released SWE-2 Flash, a coding model it says costs a fifth as much as its larger SWE-2 model and generates tokens about three times faster. Flash is built on Thinking Machines Lab’s open weight Inkling Small model, yet Cognition is keeping its own weights private, citing cybersecurity concerns. On Cognition’s own figures, Flash scored 20% on Terminal Bench 4.0 against 0.9% for the base model, and 89.9% on SWE Bench Pro v2 Hard, close to SWE-2’s 90.6%. Why it matters for tech: A model built on an open base with closed weights tests how far openness extends in practice, and whether cheaper coding models can match their larger siblings.

item.title: AI assisted proof settles a 2008 question about quantum speedups
item.description: A proof by David Turturean of Physical Superintelligence has settled the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture, open since 2008, which asks when quantum computers can gain dramatic advantages over classical machines. The proof shows that for yes or no questions on most randomly generated inputs, a classical algorithm can estimate a quantum algorithm’s answer without needing vastly more reads of the input, so large speedups need structure in the problem. The proof was found by an AI research system using a non public Anthropic model on the third day of a run, then checked in the Lean proof assistant and reviewed by researchers. Why it matters for tech: It draws a clearer line around where quantum advantage can come from, pointing algorithm research toward problems with structure worth exploiting.

item.title: UK announces fresh funding to speed up quantum commercialisation
item.description: The UK government and UK Research and Innovation have announced new funding to speed up quantum commercialisation, including £138 million for quantum sensing procurement across government, £12 million for a national commercialisation skills centre and £35 million for quantum networking testbeds. The skills centre will be run by the UK Quantum SuperConnector, a partnership led by Imperial College London with Bristol, Cambridge, Glasgow and Oxford. A UKRI review of £300 million invested between 2014 and 2024 found it helped create more than 2,000 skilled jobs, supported 74 spinout companies and attracted £482 million in private investment. Why it matters for tech: Public money is now aimed at turning research into products and jobs, and the UK is measuring a decade of funding by the companies and skills it produced.

item.title: Google hands gVisor and its agent stack to the CNCF
item.description: Google is donating gVisor, Agent Substrate and OpenRL to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, putting its AI agent infrastructure under neutral governance. gVisor, open sourced by Google in 2018, runs a lightweight kernel in user space to intercept system calls, adding isolation between containers and the host system, and is used by Anthropic and OpenAI to run untrusted code. Agent Substrate 1.0, now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine, lets agents pause when idle and resume without rebuilding their runtime, while OpenRL coordinates reinforcement learning training on a user’s own Kubernetes setup. Why it matters for tech: Sandboxing is becoming core infrastructure for agents that run untrusted code, and neutral ownership is Google’s bid to make its stack the default.

item.title: Cursor will now publish AI built apps to a live URL
item.description: Cursor has added fully managed deployment, letting its cloud agents take an AI generated app from a description to a live, shareable web address without the user setting up infrastructure. Cursor handles hosting, database provisioning and sign in, runs security checks for exposed credentials and secrets before publishing, and builds on Vercel for Platforms. The feature is available on all paid Cursor plans with cloud agents enabled, and targets internal business apps as well as personal projects. Why it matters for tech: Coding tools are closing the gap between generating an app and shipping it, which makes deployment skill less of a gate for new builders.

item.title: Chainalysis breach exposed credentials for all customers
item.description: Blockchain intelligence firm Chainalysis says an attack on its systems exposed usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all of its customers. The company, whose customers include law enforcement, government agencies and financial institutions, has taken its login portal and several products offline, including Reactor and its transaction screening tools. It says it has found no evidence that investigation data was accessed, and all users will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys before regaining access. Why it matters for tech: A breach at a firm that traces crypto crime puts its own customers’ access at risk, and the shutdown shows how much trust the service carries.

item.title: QNAP warns hackers are breaching NAS devices through Plex
item.description: QNAP says hackers are exploiting the Plex2Shell chain of four flaws in Plex Media Server to compromise its network attached storage devices, and it has received multiple reports of suspected breaches. The company urges users to update Plex Media Server to version 1.43.3.10861 through the QNAP App Center, noting that its own operating systems are not affected. Users with an exposed Plex server should treat their device and stored content as compromised, check for signs of intrusion and reinstall the operating system rather than only updating. Why it matters for tech: A media app flaw is reaching into home and small business storage, and updating alone will not clear an attack that has already landed.

item.title: IQM revenue up 51 percent as backlog passes €100 million
item.description: IQM Quantum Computers reported third quarter revenue of €8.86 million, up 50.7 percent on a year earlier, and an order backlog of €102.5 million after booking €42.2 million in new orders during the quarter. The Finnish company reaffirmed full year revenue guidance of €42 million to €47 million and closed its largest contract to date, a €33 million deal with the LUMI AI Factory. It also sold its first system in South America and a second system in Japan. Why it matters for tech: Order books are growing faster than revenue for a quantum hardware maker, which is the clearest signal yet that buyers are committing real money.

item.title: Protesters enter Microsoft data centre site in Amsterdam
item.description: About 100 protesters entered the construction site of a Microsoft data centre in Amsterdam, according to Reuters, in a protest against three 85 metre towers planned for the outskirts of the city. Amsterdam has banned new data centres until 2030, but the project dates to 2016 and proceeds as planned, with Microsoft as sole tenant. It is the latest in a week of actions against data centre building, after voters in the United States rejected data centre development in local ballots earlier in the week. Why it matters for tech: Data centre building is meeting organised local resistance in Europe as well as the US, and older approvals are letting projects proceed despite new bans.

item.title: US midterm results put data centre building under pressure
item.description: Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in the United States midterm elections on Tuesday, a result that carries direct consequences for data centre building. Voters decided 41 ballot measures about data centres across 10 states, and all but one went against data centre development, with Harwood in North Dakota the only exception. Texas, one of the largest data centre hubs, saw Democrats win races up and down the ballot, and candidates from both parties had campaigned against data centre expansion in several states. Why it matters for tech: Election results now shape where data centres can be built, turning local planning fights into a national question for the AI buildout.

item.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, a security model built to stay inside its authorised scope
item.description: OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Cyber, a model for finding exploitable vulnerabilities and developing fixes, trained to stay within the scope researchers set. It scores 48.5% on ExploitGym, up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber, and avoided out of scope services in 99.93% of alignment tests without deployment prompts. It already helped find 81 previously unknown high severity Firefox flaws, and it is initially available through the API and Codex to approved Daybreak Red customers. Why it matters for tech: Security models that can find flaws are only useful if they can be trusted not to wander, and this one pairs stronger exploit skills with measured restraint.

item.title: Google ships Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with 15 second video and a 30% price cut
item.description: Google made Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash generally available across the Gemini API and Google Cloud. It creates and edits video clips up to 15 seconds long, up from 10 seconds, with multi turn conversational editing and stronger reference consistency. The price falls 30% from version 1.1, to $0.07 per second for 720p video. Why it matters for tech: Video generation is moving from short demos toward usable ad and product clips, with editing and pricing aimed at production use.

item.title: Claude can now read your bank account, with read only access through Plaid
item.description: Anthropic launched Personal Finance in Claude in beta, connecting the chatbot to bank and card accounts through Plaid. Claude can break down spending by category, say which bills remain before payday, and judge whether a large purchase is affordable, using up to two years of transaction history. Access is read only: Claude cannot move, manage or invest money, and it does not see banking passwords. The beta is rolling out this week to Claude Pro, Max and Ultra subscribers in the US. Why it matters for tech: AI assistants are moving from answering questions to acting on personal financial data, which makes read only access and clear limits the story.

item.title: Quantinuum maps its Nexus platform toward a fault tolerant computer in 2029
item.description: Quantinuum published a roadmap to grow Nexus, its platform as a service, into a developer platform for fault tolerant quantum applications, tracking hardware releases through Apollo, its planned universal fault tolerant computer in 2029. Releases will progressively automate error correction, resource management and deployment. Nexus already serves more than 200 organisations, up 45% in 2026, with job submissions up tenfold in the year to August 2026. Why it matters for tech: Quantum vendors are now competing on developer platforms, not only hardware, so applications built today can carry over to fault tolerant machines.

item.title: IBM, Oak Ridge and AMD pair quantum hardware with supercomputing to advance error correction
item.description: IBM, the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory and AMD launched a joint co-design platform for quantum error correction, combining quantum and high performance computing. The first deployment pairs IBM quantum computers, including the 120 qubit Nighthawk processor, with Oak Ridge's Umbra system, powered by AMD Instinct MI355X GPUs and 5th Gen EPYC CPUs. The work supports the US Department of Energy goal of 100 logical qubits running 100,000 hard operations by late 2028. Why it matters for tech: Error correction needs classical computing at scale, and this platform tests quantum and supercomputing as one system rather than two separate tools.

item.title: Google donates its agent runtime stack to the CNCF as Agent Substrate hits 1.0
item.description: Google donated three open source projects that started at Google, Agent Substrate, gVisor and OpenRL, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation after their acceptance into the CNCF Sandbox. Agent Substrate, which runs isolated agent environments, reached version 1.0 and is generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine, restoring idle agents in under 500 milliseconds at 10 times container density. Why it matters for tech: Agent infrastructure is getting the same neutral, open governance treatment Kubernetes got, so no single vendor controls how agents run at scale.

item.title: OpenSSH ships emergency fix for a flaw that let long passwords bypass login on Alpine Linux
item.description: OpenSSH released version 10.6p2 to fix a critical flaw in which a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long could log in to accounts with no password set, such as key only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers. The flaw affects systems where the server checks passwords without PAM, which is how Alpine's openssh-server package is built. Alpine published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16, and no attacks using the flaw have been reported. Why it matters for tech: A password check that accepts the wrong input is a serious failure, and Alpine's wide use in containers makes fast patching matter.

item.title: FBI and CISA warn hackers are targeting refrigeration systems
item.description: The FBI and CISA warned that hackers are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems worldwide, in a joint advisory with the US health, agriculture and transport departments. Attackers exploit unpatched or internet accessible temperature controllers to alter settings, which can spoil food, damage equipment and create fire hazards. The warning follows attacks on European refrigeration systems, including controllers at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets in October. Why it matters for tech: Cyberattacks on refrigeration reach beyond data theft into food safety and public health, so operators are urged to take controllers off the public internet.

item.title: Horizon Quantum plans to buy error correction specialist Entropica Labs for $27 million
item.description: Horizon Quantum signed a non-binding letter of intent to acquire Singapore based quantum software company Entropica Labs for about $27 million in Horizon Quantum Class A ordinary shares. Entropica Labs specialises in error correction and fault tolerance. The deal still needs due diligence, audits and definitive agreements. Why it matters for tech: Quantum software firms are consolidating around error correction, the capability every hardware maker needs before fault tolerant machines arrive.

item.title: Agility Robotics lists on Nasdaq as humanoid robots face scrutiny over scale
item.description: Agility Robotics, maker of the Digit humanoid robot, listed on the Nasdaq on November 5 through a merger with a special purpose acquisition company, becoming the first dedicated humanoid robot developer to trade publicly in the US. Digit robots already work at customer sites including GXO warehouses and a Schaeffler factory, and the next model, Digit 5, arrives in 2027 with 50 pound lifting and more than 20 hours of work per day. The company's filing shows $1.8 million of revenue in 2025 against a $140 million operating loss, and notes humanoid robots remain unproven at scale. Why it matters for tech: A public listing tests whether investors will fund humanoid robots before the market proves itself, and Agility's numbers show how early that bet still is.

item.title: OpenAI drops NDAs with public officials for its data centre projects
item.description: OpenAI published a National Community Compact and a Compute Campus Policy Blueprint setting out commitments for future compute campuses it owns and operates, including paying the full cost of the electricity it uses and publishing the jobs it expects to create. It will not use non-disclosure agreements with public officials, allowing only narrow protections for security information, trade secrets or proprietary information. The announcement follows midterm votes in which US voters decided local data centre measures. Why it matters for tech: Data centre deals have drawn scrutiny over secrecy and local costs, and OpenAI is putting its community terms in writing rather than leaving them to negotiation.

item.description: An AWS Machine Learning Blog post shows how two decision models, Jev and Strands Decider, connect to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations through code based evaluators. item.title: IBM Quantum and QuICS use AI agents to find over 500 magic state factory designs
item.description: IBM Quantum and University of Maryland QuICS researchers used AI agents with deterministic solvers to discover more than 500 new magic state factories. These produce the non Clifford states that fault tolerant quantum computers need, with significantly lower resource requirements, and the detailed circuit models are openly accessible. Why it matters for tech: Magic state production is a major cost centre in fault tolerant designs, so cheaper factories change machine economics.

item.title: Superinductor built inside a silicon chip in a commercial CMOS process
item.description: A study in Nature Electronics by researchers from nanoGUNE's Quantum Hardware group, Quantum Motion and UK partners introduces a superinductor created within a silicon integrated circuit. The device was fabricated in a commercial CMOS process, the same family of processes used for ordinary chips. Why it matters for tech: Components made in standard chip processes are easier to manufacture at scale for quantum hardware.

item.title: CQMTEK raises more than $15 million to expand quantum measurement manufacturing

item.title: IonQ completes $1.15 billion acquisition of security firm Elisity
item.description: IonQ has completed its acquisition of Elisity, a zero trust security company, in an all stock transaction. IonQ's own announcement says it issued 1.15 billion US dollars of consideration in common stock at closing, with up to 150 million dollars more payable if Elisity meets revenue milestones through January 2028, and that Elisity's technology complements its post quantum cryptography and quantum key distribution work. Why it matters for tech: A quantum computing company is adding an operating security business to its revenue base.

item.title: Zyxel patches zero day used to compromise nearly 1,000 network switches
item.description: Zyxel has patched a zero day vulnerability in its GS1900 series network switches. BleepingComputer reports that attackers exploited it to compromise nearly 1,000 devices worldwide and steal configuration files and credentials. Why it matters for tech: Network switches are trusted infrastructure; stolen configurations hand attackers a map of the networks those switches protect.

item.title: Google patches critical Android flaw that needs no user interaction
item.description: Google's November security bulletin patches a critical flaw, CVE-2026-58868, that could let an attacker run code on a phone remotely without any user action. It affects Android 14 through 17, and the fix arrives at security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers distribute on their own schedules. Why it matters for tech: The gap between Google's patch and each maker's rollout is the window of exposure for most Android users.

item.title: US voters decide 41 local data centre measures in the midterm elections
item.description: Ballotpedia counted 41 local ballot measures on data centre policy across 10 states on November 3: 28 would limit development and 13 would facilitate it. In reported results, Edgewater, Florida voted to add a ban on new data centres to its city charter, Alhambra, California voted to prohibit data centres, and Harwood, North Dakota rejected its restrictive measure, the only one voted down in USA Today's tally of local results. Why it matters for tech: Local ballot outcomes now directly decide where large data centres can be built in the United States.

item.description: Google DeepMind describes agentic cheminformatics built with its Antigravity platform and a set of Cheminformatics Skills. The system searches compounds and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles, a class of molecules used in drug design. Why it matters for tech: It is a concrete case of agents doing specialist scientific work rather than only answering questions.

item.title: New benchmark finds frontier models lose track of changing facts in long documents
item.description: Allen AI's StateBench tests how well language models track information that changes across long documents, across four levels of difficulty. Frontier models including Gemini 3.8 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 handled simple updates but fell to 13 percent accuracy or lower on the hardest problems at the longest lengths, while recurrent and hybrid architectures generalised further when trained on the task. Why it matters for tech: Long document and agent work depends on exactly this state tracking, so the failure mode matters well beyond the benchmark.

item.title: Universal Quantum unveils a foundry made trapped ion processor built for modular scaling
item.description: Universal Quantum has launched the iQPU, a trapped ion processor fabricated in a foundry, with control electronics integrated on chip. Its UQConnect interconnect is designed to link multiple modules, and the processors are destined for two quantum computers being built for the German Aerospace Center. Why it matters for tech: Foundry fabrication and modular links are two of the practical steps needed to scale trapped ion machines.

item.title: One extra measurement cuts qubit errors by more than half in Regensburg experiment
item.description: Researchers at the University of Regensburg and their international partners showed that a single additional measurement before a series of quantum operations reduced the qubit error rate by more than half. The results were published in Applied Physics Reviews. Why it matters for tech: Low cost error reduction matters because error correction overhead decides how large a useful quantum machine must be.

item.title: Quint Computing raises €9.1 million seed round for hardware level quantum error correction
item.description: Quint Computing has secured €9.1 million (10.2 million US dollars) in seed funding plus a €2.2 million European Innovation Council Pathfinder grant. The company says its architecture aims to reduce physical error correction overhead by up to 100 times, using continuous electrical control in superconducting circuits. Why it matters for tech: Error correction is where quantum hardware economics are decided, and investors are funding it at the hardware layer.

item.title: IQM calls for an EU Quantum Act with dedicated qubit foundries
item.description: In a report titled Quantum Is Europe's Second Chance, IQM Quantum Computers calls on the EU to pass a Quantum Act. It proposes dedicated qubit foundries, more late stage growth capital and DARPA style procurement, arguing that Europe is strong in public investment and deployments but weaker in venture capital, chip manufacturing and regulatory speed. Why it matters for tech: The proposal shows industry shaping the EU quantum policy agenda before legislation is drafted.

item.description: OpenAI is increasing payouts under its Security Bug Bounty programme and adding bonuses tied to report quality, researcher loyalty and priority campaigns. The programme pays independent researchers who find and report vulnerabilities in OpenAI products and services. Why it matters for tech: Bigger rewards pull more skilled researchers toward finding flaws in widely used AI systems before attackers do.

item.title: Anthropic adds Claude Code limits aimed at game cloning
item.description: Anthropic has confirmed new restrictions in Claude Code that stop the tool from reproducing existing video games, after its Opus 5.5 model began blocking game recreation requests. Some users report that generic reverse engineering tasks are also being blocked, and an Anthropic employee said the company is iterating to find the right balance. Why it matters for tech: It is a live example of a model maker enforcing copyright limits inside a coding tool, with false positives already hitting legitimate work.

item.title: Experiment backs a route to more error resistant quantum information storage
item.description: Researchers have produced experimental support for the theoretical basis of topological quantum computing, an approach that stores information in special quantum states expected to be more resistant to local disturbances. The work addresses one of the field's core problems: how easily quantum information degrades. Why it matters for tech: If topological approaches hold up, they could reduce the error correction burden that dominates quantum hardware design today.

item.title: Developers choose smaller AI models on purpose, and report better results
item.description: The New Stack reports that some development teams are deliberately downgrading the AI models they use for coding work, and finding the results better for their purposes. Why it matters for tech: Model choice is becoming an engineering decision about fit and cost, not a race to the most powerful model.

item.title: Microsoft: real world exploitation concentrates in a small set of vulnerabilities
item.description: Microsoft's analysis of real world attacks finds that exploitation concentrates in a small, high impact subset of known vulnerabilities. It advises defenders to prioritise patching by exploitation likelihood, exposure and potential blast radius, rather than by severity score alone. Why it matters for tech: It gives security teams an evidence based order for patching when they cannot patch everything at once.

Why it matters for tech: It puts Apple into home robotics, a new product category for the company, at a four figure price point.

item.title: Russia plans underground data centres after Ukrainian drone strikes
item.description: Ars Technica reports that Ukrainian drone strikes on exposed Russian infrastructure have prompted Russian plans to move data centres underground. Russia's Digital Development Ministry has confirmed, as reported by Kommersant, that it completed drone protection recommendations for data centres, covering underground siting for the most critical sites, and sent them to the relevant organisations. Why it matters for tech: The conflict is directly reshaping where and how a major state builds and protects its data centre capacity.
